source.title: A unifying framework from neural superposition to sparse interpretable codes
source.authors: David A. Klindt; Charles O'Neill; P. Reizinger; Harald Maurer; N. Miolane

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a complete paper, but its body title is “From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks,” whereas the supplied title is “A unifying framework from neural superposition to sparse interpretable codes.” The body identifies itself as an arXiv preprint dated March 2025.
record.tranche_reason: This is a perspective paper about superposition, sparse coding and interpretability. Its own examples measure additivity in whole neural representation vectors, not whether individual neurons have unrelated jobs or whether feature-over-neuron capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The paper reports additivity examples for ViT-B/16 representation vectors, including a statistical result for further examples (N=10) and a cosine similarity for one analogy example. These do not measure individual-neuron polysemanticity or test its proposed capacity-pressure cause. It also discusses prior work on mixed selectivity, sparse autoencoders and virtual neurons; those cited findings are not rows.
record.test_reason: Perspective paper. Its own analyses (ViT-B/16 additivity of whole representation vectors, one analogy cosine similarity) do not measure whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, nor test capacity pressure, architecture effects or measurement dependence. The superposition-causes-polysemanticity argument (Sec. 5.3, M<N mixes more concepts per neuron) is theoretical, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors argue that classification-trained networks represent latent features up to a linear, non-orthogonal transformation (superposition), and that sparse coding can recover interpretable codes from them. They also argue that permutation-invariant quantitative interpretability metrics are needed to evaluate such codes. They flag binding, SAE amortization gaps and contextual similarity judgments as open problems.
record.recipe_differences: The paper presents a theoretical perspective and illustrative representation-additivity analyses; it does not apply the original neuron-level measurement or intervention.

fits_no_version.finding: ViT-B/16 representation vectors of combined images approximate the sum of the parts' representations. Significant over baseline in representation space (p<10^-5) but not in pixel space (p≈0.88).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Image-model representations combine concepts approximately additively (linear representation / Smolensky superposition), at the population-vector level.

record.peer_reviewed: Nature Machine Intelligence (venue stated in supplied metadata); the paper body identifies an arXiv preprint.
record.problems: The image additivity evidence is illustrative and does not characterize individual neurons. The reported N=10 result gives a p-value but no effect size or further statistical details in the supplied text. The central capacity-pressure account is theoretical rather than tested in the paper’s own neuron-level experiments.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for cited studies or cited results, including prior sparse-coding, mixed-selectivity and virtual-neuron findings. The pixel-space comparison (p ≈ 0.88 in the Figure 1 caption) is mentioned in gate_note rather than entered as a row because it is not a neural network representation.

untested.parts: No vision-model neurons examined for responses to unrelated inputs.
Argued theoretically (M<N packs concepts into neurons) but not tested empirically.
Initialization, regularization and noise as causes are not tested.
No comparison across activation functions or architectures.
No re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons.
Discusses context-dependence of human interpretability judgments (apple/orange/android example) but reports no test of how activation ranges or scoring change polysemanticity classification.

record.verdict_notes: Record's relation and tranche (discusses/T6) are accepted. The pixel-space comparison (p≈0.88) is reasonably left out as a control, though it could be recorded as the baseline contrast for r1. Cited results (Klindt et al. 2023 virtual neurons, Faruqui WIT numbers, Murphy NNSE) are correctly excluded from rows.

versions.untested_parts: No individual InceptionV1 neurons or other vision-model neurons are tested for responses to unrelated inputs.
No language-model MLP neurons or token/context response mixtures are measured.

The paper presents a theoretical account relating sparse latent variables, lower-dimensional representations and superposition, but does not test whether neurons encode more features than there are neurons or whether that causes polysemanticity.
Initialization, regularization and training noise are not tested as causes of polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
The paper does not compare neuron polysemanticity across activation functions, architectures or regularization, or test performance costs of reducing it.
No canonical polysemantic neurons are examined with improved tools to determine whether their responses share a feature.
The paper discusses limitations of human interpretability judgments, but does not test how activation ranges or explanation scores change neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Compared the representation of combined-image examples with the sum of representations of their parts; the text reports further examples, N=10.

conditions.value: further examples; figure also illustrates generated and natural images

rows.measure: Statistical significance of additivity over a calibrated baseline: cosine similarity between representations of A and B alone.
rows.baseline: Calibrated baseline: cosine similarity of the representations of A and B alone; numerical value not stated.
rows.note: The caption says the further examples support statistically significant additivity in neural representation space. This is a whole-vector result, not a measurement of individual-neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: Whole-vector additivity across N=10 examples (p<10^-5 vs calibrated baseline). This is not a measure of neuron polysemanticity. Its state against any version cannot be determined. Effect size not reported.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Compared the representation of an image containing both objects with the summed representations of the separate object images.

conditions.value: GPT-4-generated elephant, pink ball and combined elephant-and-pink-ball images

rows.note: The caption describes the combined-image representation as approximated by the sum of the two separate representations; no numerical similarity for this example is given in the text.
rows.check: Illustrative figure-only additivity example. Not a neuron-level measure.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Compared the representation of a combined natural image with the summed representations of separate images.

rows.note: The caption says additivity also holds for the natural-image example; no numerical similarity for this example is given in the text.
